name: Gastric balloon / endoscopic sleeve

card.summary: Non-surgical stomach-reduction devices and stitching procedures that produce modest to moderate weight loss, with real procedural risks.
card.aka: Intragastric balloon, Orbera, Obalon, Elipse, Spatz3, endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG), Apollo Overstitch
card.price: about $8,150 US average for a balloon (Wikipedia)
card.note: Balloons are temporary; weight is commonly regained without lifestyle change, and FDA has issued safety communications on liquid-filled balloons.

quick.overview:
An intragastric balloon is a deflated silicone balloon placed in the stomach, usually endoscopically, and filled to take up space and encourage fullness. It stays for months and is then removed. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a separate procedure in which the stomach is sutured into a narrower tube without incisions.

Both are positioned between lifestyle change and surgery for people with obesity. They appear in hardmaxx discussions as a way to lose weight without a major operation.
quick.mechanism: A balloon occupies stomach volume and slows emptying, which promotes early fullness. Research on gastric distension has shown that stretching the stomach activates satiety circuits in the brain and reduces food intake in lean and obese people. ESG uses sutures to reshape the stomach into a narrower tube.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea, vomiting, cramps and reflux. Rarer problems include ulcer, perforation and obstruction after deflation or migration. The 2022 MERIT trial of ESG reported rare serious events such as bleeding and leak. Weight regain after balloon removal is common without behavior change.

lead: An intragastric balloon (gastric balloon) is an inflatable device placed in the stomach to help with weight loss when diet and exercise have not been enough and surgery is not wanted or recommended. By taking up space it produces earlier fullness and slower gastric emptying [1]. Most devices are filled with saline, and some contain a dye that colors urine if the balloon leaks [1]. Because the balloon is temporary and removable, it is often described as a reversible step between lifestyle change and bariatric surgery.

Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a separate, incisionless procedure in which a physician uses an endoscopic suturing device to fold the stomach into a narrower tube. In July 2022 the US FDA authorized ESG with the Apollo Overstitch device for adults with BMI 30 to 50 [2]. The two approaches are grouped together as endoscopic bariatric therapies, which reviews describe as producing less weight loss than bariatric surgery but fewer complications, and more weight loss than lifestyle therapy or medications [3][4].

For appearance, the route is a direct chain: reduced stomach volume leads to smaller meals, which leads to lower body weight and body fat, which changes the body's shape and, with enough loss, the face. In looksmaxxing discussions these procedures are mentioned as hardmaxx options for people with obesity who want a large change in physique without a major operation. Published research concerns medical obesity rather than cosmetic outcomes: a 2022 randomized trial of ESG reported 13.6 percent total body weight loss at one year, and balloon studies report roughly 10 to 14 percent at 4 to 12 months, depending on the device and follow-up [1][2][5].

paras: Wikipedia and Grokipedia divide balloons into endoscopically placed, swallowable and adjustable types. Endoscopic balloons such as the single-balloon Orbera and the two-balloon ReShape Dual Balloon are placed and removed by endoscopy under sedation, usually after about six months and in some cases up to 12 [1][6]. Obalon is swallowed as a capsule and inflated with gas, in up to three balloons placed in sequence, but needs endoscopy for removal [1]. The Allurion Elipse is swallowed, filled with saline, requires no endoscopy and deflates and passes naturally after about 16 weeks; it carries a European CE mark [1]. The adjustable Spatz3 can have its volume changed during treatment and was the first intragastric balloon approved for one-year use outside the US [1][6].

ESG is not a balloon. It uses full-thickness sutures placed with an endoscope-mounted suturing device (most commonly Apollo Overstitch) to fold the greater curvature of the stomach, creating a narrower, tube-like stomach without incisions. Suture patterns such as M, Z and U have been described, and no pattern has been shown to give better weight loss [2].

A balloon occupies stomach volume and delays emptying [1]. Physiological research supports a role for distension in satiety: in a 1988 study, a water-filled balloon passed into the stomach reduced intake of a liquid lunch in four lean and four obese subjects [7]; brain imaging in 18 healthy volunteers found that gastric balloon distension activates satiety circuitry [8]; and combined stomach distension and cholecystokinin reduced food intake in humans [9]. Grokipedia also mentions hormonal effects such as lower ghrelin, though it describes that evidence as less settled [6].
For ESG, Wikipedia reports that the procedure appears to slow gastric emptying and increase fullness, and that, unlike surgical sleeve gastrectomy, it does not appear to lower ghrelin [2].

Under FDA guidance cited by Wikipedia, balloons are intended for people with BMI 30 to 40, or above 27 with a weight-related condition. Listed contraindications include inflammatory bowel disease, delayed gastric emptying, pregnancy and anticoagulant use such as warfarin [1]. Grokipedia adds prior gastric surgery, large hiatal hernia and untreated psychiatric disorders, and describes use as a bridge before bariatric surgery for people with very high BMI [6]. ESG authorization in the US covers adults with BMI 30 to 50 [2]. Reviews stress that endoscopic therapies should sit inside a multidisciplinary weight-management program with long-term follow-up [10][12].

Balloons: a 2016 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia found short-term weight loss of about 4.6 to 4.8 kg and BMI reductions of 1.3 to 1.6 kg/m2, with no associated mortality. A 2020 meta-analysis of the procedureless Elipse pooled weight loss of 12.8 percent at 4 to 6 months and 10.9 percent at 12 months, and a one-year Elipse study reported about 14 percent loss at four months with about 95 percent of it maintained at one year [1]. Grokipedia describes 6 to 15 percent total body weight loss and frequent regain after removal without sustained behavior change [6]. A 2025 review summarizes both FDA-approved endoscopic categories, balloons and endoscopic gastric remodeling, as associated with roughly 10 to 20 percent total weight loss at one year [12].

ESG: the 2022 MERIT trial randomized 209 adults with BMI 30 to 40 at nine US centers (85 to ESG plus lifestyle, 124 to lifestyle alone). At one year ESG patients lost 13.6 percent of total body weight versus 0.8 percent in controls, and about 80 percent of ESG patients improved in one or more comorbidities; at two years 68 percent kept at least a quarter of their excess weight loss [2][13]. Earlier meta-analyses reported about 16 percent total body weight loss at one year, and a five-year series reported at least 10 percent loss in 90 percent of patients [2]. Retrospective comparisons with laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy favor surgery for weight loss (about 9.7 points at one year, narrowing to 4.8 at three years), while ESG shows less reflux and fewer adverse events [2]. A combination study with liraglutide reported about 25 percent loss at seven months versus 20 percent with ESG alone; studies with semaglutide or tirzepatide are lacking [2]. A 2024 analysis based on MERIT modeled the cost-effectiveness of ESG versus lifestyle modification for US commercial payers [14].

With balloons, Wikipedia lists nausea, vomiting, reflux, cramps, bloating and diarrhea as common, mostly early in treatment, and esophagitis, gastric ulcer and perforation as rare. Deflation and migration can cause bowel obstruction, and endoscopic placement and anesthesia carry procedural risks, very rarely including death. The Elipse reported 0.2 percent serious adverse events [1]. The article references an FDA safety communication on liquid-filled balloon systems [1]. The first FDA-approved device, the Garren-Edwards Bubble, was withdrawn after complications [1], and Grokipedia describes the withdrawal as following serious complications and deaths [6].

With ESG, mild to moderate GI symptoms such as nausea, cramping and bloating occur in over 70 percent of patients and usually resolve within about a week. Serious events are rare: hospitalization for pain or nausea 1.08 percent, upper GI bleeding 0.56 percent, perigastric leak or infected collection 0.48 percent, and pulmonary embolism and perforation 0.06 percent each. Wikipedia reports no deaths in the published literature [2].

The balloon concept has roots in a 1938 review linking bezoars to weight loss. A. Henning tried a balloon in a 1979 self-experiment, Nieben and Harboe used free-floating balloons in 1982, and in 1984 Percival presented a balloon diet using inflated mammary implants [1]. The Garren-Edwards Bubble became the first FDA-approved balloon in 1985 and was withdrawn about seven years later. No new device was approved until 2015, when the ReShape Dual Balloon and Orbera were cleared and Elipse received CE approval [1]. EnteroMedics acquired ReShape Medical in 2017 for about $38 million [1]. Grokipedia reports Obalon FDA approval in 2016, its withdrawal from the market after 2020, and Spatz3 approval in 2021 [6].

ESG grew out of endoluminal vertical gastroplasty (around 2008) and a suction-based suturing approach tested in the TRIM trial (2010 to 2012). The first human ESG was performed in 2012 by Dr. Christopher Thompson, and a first-in-man trial starting in April 2012 across centers in five countries refined the full-thickness suturing technique [2][15]. FDA authorization followed in July 2022 [2].

Balloons are approved in many countries, including Australia, Canada, Mexico, India, and several in Europe and South America. The average US cost is about $8,150 and is usually not covered by insurance; the European average is about EUR 3,000 [1]. Grokipedia gives ranges of $6,000 to $9,000 in the US and EUR 3,000 to 5,000 in Europe, noting Medicare and Medicaid generally do not cover balloons [6].

MERIT is the first randomized controlled trial of ESG for obesity [2][13]. Balloon evidence comes from meta-analyses and device studies reporting weight loss in people with obesity [1][12]. Registered trials include a 12-month adjustable balloon versus a 6-month fixed balloon (44 participants) [16], preoperative balloon use before gastric bypass in 314 patients [17], balloon effects on obstructive sleep apnea in 60 patients [18], a pilot in obese adolescents [19], a 131-patient trial combining botulinum toxin injection with balloon placement [20], and a bariatric endoscopy study in fatty liver disease [21]. Summary results for these registrations are not given here. No study has tested balloons or ESG for cosmetic or facial outcomes.

Lower body weight and body fat
angle.text: Endoscopic stomach-reduction procedures are used by people with obesity to lose a substantial share of body weight without incisions or, with balloons, without permanent change to the stomach. People who lose weight this way commonly describe changes in body shape and facial fat alongside the health effects.
